chapters.title: Which ideas make it into the title?
chapters.dek: Follow three phrases across twenty-five years of research to see when authors put reform, motivation and representation in the foreground.

steps.heading: Start with three phrases authors use
steps.text: Across 7,338 papers from 2001 to 2025, we track titles that name New Public Management, public service motivation or representative bureaucracy. Each cell shows the number and share of titles matching a phrase within a five-year period.

steps.heading: New Public Management appears most often early on
steps.text: The phrase appears in 19 of 939 titles in 2001–2005 and in 5 of 2,016 in 2021–2025. A 2002 Governance article names it directly in a comparison of Danish and Swedish welfare-state reforms.

steps.heading: Public service motivation peaks in the middle of the record
steps.text: Matches rose from 12 in 2006–2010 to 42 in 2011–2015, the highest count and share across the five windows. A 2009 research note used the phrase in a paper about testing the structure of public service motivation in Korea.

steps.heading: Representative bureaucracy appears more often after 2015
steps.text: The phrase rose from 5 matches in the first five years to 23 in the last five, from 0.5% to 1.1% of titles. A 2018 article pairs it with a question about performance in South Africa.

steps.heading: Each phrase tells a different story
steps.text: Reform language receded in titles, motivation peaked in the middle window, and representation appeared more often in the final two windows. The counts track the exact phrases. Papers can develop the same ideas under other wording or name them in the abstract or full text.

chapters.title: How do the five journals differ?
chapters.dek: Keep the map fixed and change the journal to see which research themes each publication emphasises.

steps.heading: Compare five journals on a shared map
steps.text: The comparison uses 7,338 papers published between 2001 and 2025, when all five current journal titles overlap. Every paper keeps its position as the view changes from one journal to another.

steps.heading: Governance is concentrated in comparative reform
steps.text: Comparative Governance and Administrative Reform contains 303 of the journal’s 970 papers, or 31.2%. Bureaucratic Discretion and Accountability accounts for another 245 papers, or 25.3%.

steps.heading: Public Management Review is concentrated in collaboration
steps.text: Collaborative Governance and Citizen Participation contains 479 of the journal’s 1,623 papers, or 29.5%. Workforce, leadership and representation papers make up another 16.8%.

steps.heading: Compare the proportions directly
steps.text: Collaboration and participation accounts for 29.5% of Public Management Review papers and 6.7% of Governance papers. The comparison uses each journal’s own total, so differences in publication volume do not determine the shares.

steps.heading: Comparative reform also anchors Public Administration
steps.text: Comparative reform is the largest group in both Governance and Public Administration. It accounts for 31.2% of Governance and 27.3% of Public Administration. The same four groups in the table let you compare their wider profiles.

steps.heading: The same themes recur across journals
steps.text: All five journals contain papers in the four groups shown here. Among these groups, workforce research has the largest share in both JPART and Public Administration Review. The titles and available abstracts guide the atlas’s assignments.

chapters.title: Which methods do authors name in titles?
chapters.dek: Track the publication language behind case studies, experiments and evidence syntheses.

steps.heading: Read the design words authors put up front
steps.text: We look for specific title phrases in the same five publication windows. Each cell shows the number and share of papers whose titles match those wording rules. A paper can contribute to several series, and a title may leave the design to the abstract or methods section.

steps.heading: Case-study language appears from the start
steps.text: Case-study wording appears in 16 of 939 titles in 2001–2005 and 11 of 2,016 in 2021–2025. A 2009 Governance article names a case study when framing research on strategic planning in the European Commission.

steps.heading: Experiment phrases become more visible
steps.text: Titles with the experiment phrases tracked here increase from one match in 2006–2010 to 28 in 2016–2020 and 40 in 2021–2025. A 2019 study of welfare attitudes in South Korea explicitly calls itself a survey experiment.

steps.heading: Evidence synthesis becomes easier to spot
steps.text: The tracked review and meta-analysis phrases appear in 4 titles in 2011–2015, 11 in 2016–2020 and 30 in 2021–2025. A 2017 JPART article names meta-analysis in its title and uses it to frame two decades of research on public service motivation.

steps.heading: Selected causal design terms are rare in titles
steps.text: We look for titles that name difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity or instrumental variables. Two titles match in 2016–2020 and two in 2021–2025. Estimating the prevalence of these designs would require coding the methods from the articles.

steps.heading: What changed is the language in the title
steps.text: Experiment and synthesis phrases appear more often in the latest window, where they account for about 2.0% and 1.5% of titles respectively. The rise shows how often authors use these phrases in the title across the five journals.

chapters.title: Where do methods and research topics overlap?
chapters.dek: Put case-study and experiment wording on the same map, then compare how often it appears within four research themes.

steps.heading: Locate titles that name case studies
steps.text: The highlighted papers use the tracked case-study wording. One is a Governance article on implementing public management reforms in the European Commission, located in Comparative Governance and Administrative Reform.

steps.heading: Switch to titles that name experiments
steps.text: The same coordinates now show titles with the tracked experiment phrases. A South Korean survey experiment on welfare attitudes sits in Public Workforces, Leadership and Representation under the atlas’s grouping.

steps.heading: Experiment wording is more common in two of these themes
steps.text: The experiment phrases occur in 29 of 849 Digital Government and Performance Management titles and 21 of 1,026 Workforce, Leadership and Representation titles. The corresponding counts are 1 of 1,066 in comparative reform and 4 of 1,097 in collaboration and participation.

steps.heading: Case-study wording is more common in comparative reform
steps.text: The case-study phrases occur in 20 of 1,066 comparative reform titles and 16 of 1,097 collaboration and participation titles. They appear in 4 of 849 digital and performance titles and 3 of 1,026 workforce and representation titles.

steps.heading: Read the overlap as a description of the corpus
steps.text: The rates describe where specific method phrases and atlas themes occur together. Titles help create the theme assignments and supply the phrase matches, so the two measurements share an input. The comparison cannot establish that methods shape the questions scholars choose.
